paragraphs.heading: What radioactivity is
paragraphs.text: Radioactive decay is the process in which an unstable atomic nucleus sheds energy as radiation. Any material that contains unstable nuclei counts as radioactive. Three of the most common kinds of decay are alpha, beta and gamma decay. The weak force drives beta decay; the electromagnetic and nuclear forces govern alpha and gamma decay.

paragraphs.heading: Random, yet predictable
paragraphs.text: For one single atom, decay happens at random. Quantum theory says there is no way to tell when a given atom will decay, no matter how long it has already existed. Yet a large number of identical atoms follow an overall decay rate, which can be stated as a decay constant or as a half-life. Half-lives vary enormously, from almost instant to far longer than the age of the universe.

paragraphs.heading: One element into another
paragraphs.text: The nucleus that decays is called the parent, and the decay yields at least one daughter nuclide. Apart from gamma decay and internal conversion, decay changes the nucleus so the daughter holds a different number of protons, neutrons or both. When the proton count changes, the atom becomes a different chemical element.

paragraphs.heading: Radioactivity in nature
paragraphs.text: Earth has 28 naturally occurring radioactive elements, made up of 35 radionuclides that are older than the Solar System. These 35 are called primordial radionuclides. Uranium and thorium are the familiar examples, along with long-lived ones such as potassium-40. Each heavy primordial radionuclide belongs to one of four decay chains.

paragraphs.heading: A blackened plate
paragraphs.text: Henri Becquerel discovered radioactivity in 1896 while working with phosphorescent materials, which glow in the dark after being exposed to light. He wrapped a photographic plate in black paper and set various phosphorescent salts on top. Nothing happened until he tried uranium salts, which darkened the plate even through the paper. In 1897 Marie Curie began studying this radiation and showed that it was a property of atoms.

paragraphs.heading: Solving the puzzle
paragraphs.text: Where the energy came from was a mystery, and if atoms were the source they had to change as they gave off rays. In 1900 Curie framed the choice as two equally unlikely options: either energy was not conserved, or elements could turn into other elements. Rutherford saw that all such elements decay by the same exponential formula, and with his student Frederick Soddy he realized that many decays transform one element into another. Searching uranium ores, Pierre and Marie Curie also isolated two new elements, polonium and radium, and coined the word radioactivity.
